title: Simplicity
subtitle: Reduce the behavior and coupling that operators must reason about
summary: Simplicity supports reliability by reducing the amount of behavior that must be understood, tested, and changed safely. Essential complexity belongs to the problem; accidental complexity comes from chosen implementations and can often be removed. Predictable code, small APIs, and clear component responsibilities make failures easier to locate. Dead code and obsolete flags are liabilities even when they appear inactive, because they retain confusing and potentially executable paths. Version control provides a way to recover deleted code without leaving it embedded in production. Modularity also applies to releases and data formats: compatible interfaces let teams change one component without rebuilding the whole system. Small, understandable releases make effects easier to attribute and allow stability and development speed to reinforce each other.

concepts.title: Essential and accidental complexity
concepts.body: Essential complexity is imposed by the problem being solved; accidental complexity arises from how the solution is built. Serving correct results under load is a real requirement, while unnecessary layers or awkward implementation choices may add avoidable difficulty. SRE should challenge the latter because every extra behavior complicates diagnosis, testing, and change without necessarily delivering value to users.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A service still needs authorization, but three overlapping authorization configuration mechanisms may be removable complexity.

concepts.title: Delete dead behavior
concepts.body: Unused code and permanently disabled features retain maintenance and reasoning costs. A flag may later change, reviving an untested path, while commented code distracts readers and becomes stale. After checking that a path is no longer needed, deletion removes those liabilities. Version history preserves the old implementation if future investigation requires it; production source need not serve as its archive.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Remove the retired exporter and its flag after verifying no supported deployment uses them.

concepts.title: Small APIs and coherent modules
concepts.body: A small API exposes only the operations needed for a clear purpose, reducing the surface that callers and maintainers must understand. Components with coherent responsibilities can be changed independently. Compatibility and versioning extend this independence across releases, avoiding a forced system-wide upgrade whenever one participant changes. A miscellaneous utility service with unrelated duties weakens that separation.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A backward-compatible schema addition lets one service upgrade while its callers migrate later.

concepts.title: Small releases improve attribution
concepts.body: A large release mixes many potential explanations for any performance or correctness change. Smaller releases narrow the set of suspects and make rollback or repair easier to reason about. Simple release procedures also help developers move faster because the effect of a change is visible sooner. The objective is understandable, controllable change rather than freezing a production system indefinitely.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Deploying one cache-policy change makes a new latency regression easier to attribute than deploying fifty unrelated changes.

misconceptions.claim: Disabled code has no operational cost.
misconceptions.correction: It can confuse maintainers and later become active without being adequately tested.

misconceptions.claim: Simplicity means never changing a stable service.
misconceptions.correction: Small, isolated, predictable changes can improve both agility and stability.

scenario.title: Delete a risky option
scenario.context: A service has a legacy configuration flag that changes timeout behavior, is undocumented, and is never used in current traffic. Keeping it complicates testing.

options.label: Remove the dead flag after checking dependencies
options.benefit: The state space shrinks and the remaining behavior is easier to reason about.
options.cost: A hidden consumer would need a migration path.
options.consequence: The team searches callers, announces removal, and deletes the flag.

options.label: Keep every option for compatibility
options.benefit: An unknown consumer is less likely to break.
options.cost: The unsupported path keeps complexity and failure modes alive.
options.consequence: The flag remains and every future change must test it.

scenario.debrief: Deleting an unused mode reduces the state space after compatibility is checked; keeping it preserves a hypothetical consumer at a permanent complexity cost.

quiz.question: What is the strongest reason to delete a permanently retired feature instead of hiding it behind a flag?
options: Deletion removes a dormant behavior that could return unexpectedly
Version control cannot store inactive code
quiz.explanation: Dead paths still complicate reasoning and can be reactivated accidentally.

quiz.question: How does API compatibility support reliability?
options: It removes the need to test clients
It permits independent component upgrades without forcing a simultaneous system-wide change
It guarantees every future API can remain unchanged
quiz.explanation: Compatible interfaces reduce coupling between release schedules.

quiz.question: A release contains 100 unrelated changes and latency worsens. Which practice would make the next regression easier to diagnose?
quiz.explanation: Fewer simultaneous changes reduce ambiguity about the cause of the observed effect.

exercise.title: Remove one unnecessary behavior
exercise.prompt: Choose an obsolete feature flag or interface. Explain how to establish that it is unused, remove it, and verify that supported callers still work.
